To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the temperature‐independent homogeneous linewidth of the F center emission in CaO is due to scattering of pseudolocaiized phonons, and that the zero‐photon emission peaking at λ=571.1 nm is not due to F centers.

the homogeneous broadening of a phosphorescent F center in CaF2 is due to elastic scattering of pseudophonons, that these pseudophonons also couple the Jahn-Teller components of the photoexcited state of this defect, and that the zero‐frequency emission of F centers in CaF2 does not originate in this defect but is probably due to a different defect.

the temperature‐induction homogeneous broadening of phosphorescent emission lines of the F center is caused by pseudolocalized elastic scattering phonons, which also dynamically couple the J–T components of this defect in the photoexcitated 3T1 u state.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the energy and phase relaxation processes of the phosphorescent F center in CaF2.
the energy and phase relaxation of the F center.
the study of the energy relaxation and phase relaxation processes of the F center.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the F center is a phosphorescent center in CaO, but the zero‐phononspectrum of this phosphorescence does not originate in this center.
the F center is a very interesting defect in CaO, and that its optical properties have not yet been completely understood.

in the 0.1–300 K temperature range the F‐center emission spectrum is dominated by the emission of the 2T1u component of the F center, and the 2Eg component is only visible in the 1.2–2.0 eV region of the absorption spectrum.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 3T1→1A1 transition in the F center is a Jahn–Tellertype process involving a 90 cm−l phonon.
the F center in alkaline earth oxides is a complex system with a rich spectroscopy.
in CaO the F centers are not the only species responsible for the phosphorescence at 571.2 nm.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the F center in calcium oxide is not an ideal system for studying electron–phonon interactions.
the F center can be used as a probe for studying the dynamics of pseudolocal phonons in a solid.

a careful analysis of the temperature‐indition broadening of the emission spectrum of phosphorescent defects can yield valuable insight into the nature of the defect and its coupling to the phonon bath.
